name: Ósósọ̀
confidence_why: The quoted passage has not been checked against the cited source.
catalog_citation: Legbeti, Agnes Temitope. 2024. Ósósọ̀ Orthography: A Proposal. Journal of West African Languages 51(1): 91-103.
catalog_locator: sec. 5.3 'On the issue of Tone and Orthography', p. 99; cf. sec. 4 'The Sound System of Ósósọ̀', pp. 93-97, and sec. 5.2 p. 98 (only token of 'stress')
catalog_quote: Following the Tone Economy Principle of Williamson (1984:42), the most common tone should be left unmarked. Ósósọ̀ is a two-tone language (high and low), with the low tone having higher frequency of occurrence – it occurs in monosyllabic, disyllabic, and polysyllabic forms. On this premise, I propose that only the high tone should be marked (bearing in mind that high tone changes inherent low on nouns + noun as marker of possession) and largely where ambiguity will result if unmarked. ... All scientific academic works should, however, apply full tone marks on materials containing Ósósọ̀ data.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ososo is described as a lexical tone language with two tones (High, Low), L being the more frequent; a grammatical H replaces inherent L on nouns in N+N possessive constructions. The source's phonology section (segments, tone) makes no mention of word stress or accent, so no stress placement rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal alternation noted: 'high tone changes inherent low on nouns + noun as marker of possession'.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/grammatical tone on words; author's own fieldwork (10 speakers, Ibadan 400 wordlist, narratives) and her 2022 Ibadan PhD on Ososo tone. No word- or phrase-level stress discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Ósósọ̀ [ósósɔ̀] of Ososo town, Akoko-Edo LGA, Edo State (ISO oso, Glottolog osos1238; the author cites the glottocode herself). Exonym Ọ́sọ́sọ̀. No dialect differentiation mentioned. Author classifies it as North-Central Edoid (following Elugbe 1989/Lewis 2013), whereas Glottolog 5.x files it under Northwestern Edoid > Igwic; same language either way.

sources.note: Sec.4 'The Sound System of Ósósọ̀' (46 speech sounds, consonant classes incl. lenis /bh mh dh/, minimal pairs, vowels); sec.5.3 p.99: 'Ósósọ̀ is a two-tone language (high and low), with the low tone having higher frequency of occurrence'. Nothing on word stress/accent; the only occurrence of 'stress' (p.98) is a generic remark that punctuation cues in speech are 'universally signaled by pitch, volume, stress, pause'.
